papers.title: Neurosurgical Manifestations of Rheumatologic Diseases: Clinical, Imaging, and Surgical Implications.
papers.abstract: This article reviews the neurosurgical considerations and clinical manifestations of giant cell arteritis, rheumatoid arthritis-related cervical spine disease, ankylosing spondylitis, systemic lupus erythematosus, neurosarcoidosis, and Lyme disease. Across these disease entities, neurosurgical urgency typically reflects inflammatory vascular compromise, skeletal instability, occult fracture with secondary neurologic deficits, or mass-like and meningeal phenotypes that mimic malignancy or infection. The article emphasizes pattern-based triage, high-yield imaging selection, and the limited scenarios requiring neurosurgical intervention including stabilization, CSF diversion, decompression, or biopsy.
papers.journal: Rheumatic diseases clinics of North America

papers.title: Incidence and Factors of Bacterial Zoonotic Infection in Solid Organ Transplant Recipients.
papers.abstract: Infection remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality among solid organ transplant (SOT) recipients, yet zoonotic pathogens as a distinct category remain underrecognized. We investigated the incidence, and risk factors of bacterial zoonotic infections after transplantation using a large multicenter database. We queried the TriNetX database in from 2014-2024 to identify adult SOT recipients who developed bacterial zoonotic infections. We identified twelve bacterial zoonoses using ICD-10 codes: anthrax, brucellosis, cat scratch disease, glanders, leprosy, leptospirosis, tularemia, parrot fever, pasteurellosis, plague, Q fever, and rat-bite fever. Sixty-one SOT recipients (0.03%) developed a bacterial zoonotic infection, corresponding to an incidence of 4.87 per 100 000 person-years. The median time from transplantation to infection was 736 days (IQR, 298-1970), with 72.1% of infections occurring more than one year after transplantation. The hospitalization rate was 41.0%, and the 90-day all-cause mortality rate was 6.6%. The three most common infections were Q fever, cat scratch disease, and pasteurellosis. No cases of anthrax, tularemia, plague, or rat-bite fever were identified. Black recipients had a 49% lower risk of bacterial zoonotic infection than White recipients. Bacterial zoonotic infections were uncommon and occurred predominantly during the late post-transplant period. The lower risk observed among Black recipients reflects differences in animal and environmental exposure that this study could not measure, rather than biological susceptibility. Animal safety counseling should extend beyond the early post-transplant period and continue as part of long-term post-transplant care.

papers.title: Comprehensive Assessment of Babesia gibsoni Infection in Dogs: Clinicopathological, Imaging, and Oxidative Stress Perspectives.
papers.abstract: The present study investigated clinico-pathological alterations associated with naturally occurring Babesia gibsoni infection in dogs from Mizoram, India. Diagnosis was established using rapid antibody detection, microscopic blood smear examination, and polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Blood samples were collected to study the haemogram, and serum samples were used for the evaluation of serum biochemical profile and oxidant-antioxidant indices. Abdominal ultrasonography was performed in the infected dogs. Of 138 samples screened, 43 (31.15%), 70 (50.72%), and 85 (61.59%) were positive by rapid antibody test, blood smear examination, and PCR, respectively. The most consistent clinical signs included depression/lethargy, inappetence/anorexia, and pyrexia. Splenomegaly and splenic lesions were the most consistent ultrasonographic findings noticed. Major haemato-biochemical alterations comprised anaemia, leukocytosis with neutrophilia and eosinophilia, thrombocytopaenia, hypoproteinaemia, hypoalbuminaemia, hyperbilirubinaemia, azotaemia, and increased alanine aminotransferase (ALT), alkaline phosphatase (ALP), and C-reactive protein (CRP) levels. Dogs with B. gibsoni infection exhibited significantly (P < 0.001) higher lipid peroxide (LPO) levels and significantly (P < 0.001) lower total antioxidant capacity (T-AOC) and reduced glutathione (GSH). Red blood cell (RBC) count showed a negative correlation with LPO (r = - 0.741; P < 0.01) and a positive correlation with GSH (r = 0.714; P < 0.01) and T-AOC (r = 0.828; P < 0.01), indicating a role of oxidant-antioxidant imbalance in the severity of anaemia. These findings underscore the multiorgan involvement of the disease and suggest a potential role of oxidative stress in the pathogenesis of B. gibsoni-induced anaemia in dogs.

papers.title: Tick-borne pathogens in Finnish wildlife: The role of non-native raccoon dog and European hare.
papers.abstract: The role of different host species in the circulation dynamics of tick-borne pathogens (TBPs) in northern ecosystems remains insufficiently characterized, despite the widespread distribution of these pathogens in European wildlife. In particular, the contribution of medium-sized mammals, including non-native species, to TBP circulation is poorly understood. We screened 446 skin samples from nine wildlife species in Finland for multiple zoonotic TBPs to assess pathogen occurrence across host species with particular emphasis on the invasive raccoon dog (Nyctereutes procyonoides) and non-native European hare (Lepus europaeus). Borrelia burgdorferi s.l., Anaplasma phagocytophilum, and Rickettsia helvetica were the most frequently detected pathogens, with prevalence varying among host species. Babesia spp. was predominantly detected in ungulates, whereas Spiroplasma ixodetis and Borrelia miyamotoi were rare. Raccoon dogs and European hares showed generally low pathogen prevalence, while the highest TBP prevalences were observed in squirrels, hedgehogs, and ungulates. We also screened for two Ixodes-associated endosymbionts (Rickettsiella spp. and Midichloria mitochondrii) as potential indicators of tick exposure. Although Rickettsiella spp. was associated with TBP infections, the low prevalence of both endosymbionts suggests their limited utility as tick bite markers. These findings provide a cross-sectional overview of TBP occurrence in Finnish wildlife and demonstrate that host-pathogen associations vary among species. The relatively low pathogen prevalence observed in the raccoon dog and European hare suggests that these species are unlikely to play a major role in maintaining TBP transmission in northern ecosystems, although they may contribute to tick abundance and dispersal.

papers.title: Identifying counties at elevated acarological risk for reporting high incidence of Lyme disease in the eastern United States.
papers.abstract: Lyme disease, caused primarily by the bite of a nymphal blacklegged tick (Ixodes scapularis) infected with Borrelia burgdorferi sensu stricto (Bbss), is the most common vector-borne disease in the United States. Counties reporting high Lyme disease incidence (LDI) continue to expand beyond historic foci in the Northeast and Upper Midwest. Identifying areas of expansion aids in targeting efforts to improve Lyme disease awareness in affected communities. Tick surveillance is conducted to track changes in acarological risk for tickborne diseases; the density of host-seeking Bbss-infected I. scapularis nymphs (DIN) is considered the most predictive metric for human LDI. We aimed to identify a threshold in DIN that accurately separated high (≥10 average annual cases/100,000 and ≥3 cases/year; 2022-2023) from low LDI counties in the eastern US. Using previously reported model-derived DIN, we identified 0.98 Bbss-infected nymphs per 1000 m2 as the threshold. Based on this threshold, we classified 18% of eastern counties (487/2695), primarily in the Northeast and Upper Midwest, with both high LDI and elevated acarological risk and 72% (1935/2695) with both low LDI and acarological risk. Another 8% of counties (220/2695), primarily in Michigan, Illinois, Indiana, and Ohio, were predicted to pose elevated acarological risk, but reported low LDI and may reflect areas of emergence that could benefit from expanded tick surveillance and public health outreach. The remaining 2% of counties (53/2695), mainly along the Appalachian Mountains, reported high LDI, but were misclassified as low acarological risk, highlighting the need for additional tick surveillance to improve acarological risk assessments.

papers.title: Untitled
papers.abstract: The Lyme disease spirochete, Borrelia burgdorferi, maintains a low burden during vertebrate infection. This limitation has historically proven to be particularly challenging for genome-based studies of B. burgdorferi infection and spirochete presence after antibiotic treatment. Here, we used TBDCapSeq, an oligo capture-based next- generation sequencing assay, to demonstrate its utility for genome recovery of B. burgdorferi directly from C3H- and BALB/c-infected mice. Tissue fragments from the ear, heart, tarsus, and infection-site skin were collected at 3 and 6 months post-tick infection from antibiotic-treated and untreated animals. We evaluated 59 tissues from 20 untreated mice and 48 tissues from 17 doxycycline-treated mice for spirochete burden and extent of genome recovery. In the untreated mice, genome recovery from each tissue was determined by the amount of borrelial DNA present in the sequencing library and was highest in the ear and heart, followed by the skin, and lowest in the tarsus. We established that approximately 50% of the genome could be recovered with as few as 10 spirochetes per assay and >90% recovery could be achieved with only 35 spirochete genomes. In the antibiotic-treated mice, trace quantities of fragmented Borrelia DNA were still present in tissues at 3 and 6 months. However, none of the tissue samples from these mice yielded an intact B. burgdorferi genome characteristic of a viable spirochete. Combined, our findings demonstrate that capture sequencing enables genomic analyses of B. burgdorferi directly within animal hosts.IMPORTANCELyme disease, caused by the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi, is the most common tick-borne infection in the United States. Low pathogen burden is a major limitation of B. burgdorferi studies in animal hosts and humans that has impacted a wide range of studies ranging from diagnostics, evolutionary analyses, and pathogenesis. It has also contributed to the controversies regarding B. burgdorferi persistence after antibiotic treatment. We show that a next-generation capture sequencing-based approach can readily overcome the current limitations of B. burgdorferi genomic analyses within animal hosts. We successfully recovered abundant genomic information directly from mouse tissues, and we did not find genetic evidence of intact bacteria present after antibiotic treatment. This approach can be employed to gain further insights into B. burgdorferi and provide critical genome data during animal and human infection.

papers.title: One Health genomic surveillance of ticks found on community-dwelling non-human 'farm' animals to identify microbes associated with tick borne illnesses in Eastern Ontario.
papers.abstract: Companion animals, such as dogs and cats, and wildlife are recognized as sentinel species in One Health surveillance due to periodic exposure to ticks and infection by tick-borne pathogens (TBPs). Surveillance of this type is a strategy that captures a broad range of genetic, immunological, and behavioral factors that affect tick and disease dynamics. In contrast, non-human animals (hereafter referred to as 'animals') that are traditionally farmed for their meat and other products have been largely overlooked as sentinel species. Community-dwelling farm sanctuary residents, such as cattle, pigs, horses, and other traditionally 'farmed' animals have close daily contact with human caregivers, making them excellent candidates for One Health surveillance. These animals, often free-range in pastures and/or woodlands, bridging the territory inhabited by wildlife and that occupied by humans. This study collected 67 ticks, from bovines (n = 22), equines (n = 35) and canines (n = 6) residing in a farm animal sanctuary and screened them for microbes associated with tick borne illnesses using 16S rRNA V4 amplicon targeted sequencing (515F/906R) with custom Rickettsia buchneri blocking primers to boost sensitivity. Only 60 ticks were viable for analysis, 59 were of Ixodes species and one was Dermacentor variabilis. Of these, 31.6% (n = 19) tested positive for potential pathogens, including 21.6% (n = 13) for the causative agent of Lyme disease (Borrelia burgdorferi) and 15% (n = 9) for Anaplasma phagocytophilum, with a co-infection rate of five percent (n = 3). Utilizing community dwelling sanctuary residents allowed us to detect potential threats to both animal and human health and was instrumental in the rapid diagnosis of anaplasmosis in two study participants (a horse and a pony) who showed symptoms of lethargy and inappetence after being bitten by ticks.

papers.title: Molecular detection of Bartonella dromedarii-like in Microthoracius spp. (Phthiraptera: Microthoraciidae) associated with alpacas from the southern Andes of Peru.
papers.abstract: Blood-sucking insects, such as lice, act as potential vectors of vector-borne pathogens. The proposed study aimed to diagnose molecularly Bartonella sp., an arthropod-borne bacterium in Microthoracius lice collected from alpacas in Peru. Ninety-six lice of the Microthoracius genus were collected from alpaca crias from the Quenamari and Chillihua communities from Cuzco, Peru. All lice were molecularly analyzed by PCR protocols for Bartonella sp. Bartonella genus detection was performed by amplifying the 16S-23S internal transcribed spacer (ITS) region. Bartonella species were identified amplifying the citrate synthase gene (gltA), the RNA polymerase beta-subunit gene (rpoB), and the cell division protein gene (ftsZ). Bartonella DNA was detected in 33.3% (32/96) lice. M. mazzai had the highest Bartonella prevalence (50%; 10/20), followed by M. praelongiceps (28.9%; 22/76). Sequencing of PCR products of fragments of the gltA, rpoB, and ftsZ genes showed homology of 100%, 99.8-100%, and 99.4-99.9%, respectively, with Bartonella dromedarii. No statistical association was observed between B. dromedarii-like detection and louse species and communities. This study records for the first time the occurrence of Bartonella in alpaca lice and suggests that these insects may act as potential vectors for these pathogens, but further, more detailed studies are required. As Microthoracius lice are common camelid ectoparasites, future studies will be necessary to understand the situation of bartonellosis by B. dromedarii-like in domestic and wild South American camelids in various regions of the Peruvian Andes.
papers.journal: Comparative immunology, microbiology and infectious diseases

papers.title: Molecular detection and characterization of flea-associated bacteria: genetic diversity and co-occurrence patterns involving Bartonella, Rickettsia, and Wolbachia in Ctenocephalides felis felis from an Atlantic Forest region of Brazil.
papers.abstract: Ctenocephalides felis felis is a widespread ectoparasite of dogs and cats and has been associated with transmission of several microorganisms of veterinary and public health relevance. This study investigated the molecular occurrence, genetic diversity, and co-occurrence patterns of Bartonella spp., Rickettsia spp., and Wolbachia spp. in fleas collected from dogs and cats in an Atlantic Forest area encompassing the Ilhéus and Itabuna microregions, Bahia State, northeastern Brazil. A total of 1,489 fleas were analyzed, including 1,301 collected from 81 dogs and 188 from 39 cats. PCR targeting the endogenous cox1 gene successfully amplified DNA from 95.77% of fleas collected from dogs and 97.34% of those collected from cats. Quantitative PCR (qPCR) targeting the 16S-23S rRNA internal transcribed spacer (ITS) revealed a higher molecular detection rate of Bartonella spp. in fleas from cats (34.43%) than in those from dogs (8.98%). Conversely, Rickettsia spp. was detected more frequently in fleas collected from dogs (24.8%) than from cats (3.28%). Wolbachia spp. was more frequently detected in female fleas from both dogs (52.8%) and cats (50.3%) than in male fleas (p < 0.05). Triple co-occurrence of the three microorganisms was detected in 0.08% (11/1246) of flea DNA samples positive the cox-1 endogenous gene and subjected to downstream molecular analyses for Bartonella spp., Rickettsia spp., and Wolbachia spp.. Phylogenetic analyses based on multiple molecular markers for Bartonella spp. (gltA, ftsZ, nuoG, and rpoB), Rickettsia spp. (gltA, htrA, ompA, and ompB), and Wolbachia spp. (gatB and wsp) confirmed the detection of Bartonella henselae, Bartonella clarridgeiae, Rickettsia felis, and Wolbachia spp. belonging to supergroups B and F. In fleas collected from dogs, the detection of Wolbachia spp. was associated with a higher predicted probability of Rickettsia spp. detection, whereas in fleas collected from cats it was associated with a lower predicted probability of Bartonella spp. detection. Overall, the findings revealed distinct host-associated molecular detection patterns of Bartonella spp., Rickettsia spp., and Wolbachia spp. in C. felis felis, demonstrating the circulation and genetic diversity of these bacterial agents in flea populations. The detection of zoonotic bacterial agents in fleas highlights their relevance for integrated veterinary and public health surveillance within a One Health framework.

papers.title: Zinc Metalloproteases of Apicomplexan Parasites: Conserved Targets for Broad-Spectrum Antiparasitic Drug Discovery.
papers.abstract: The phylum Apicomplexa includes major protozoan pathogens of humans and animals (Plasmodium falciparum, Toxoplasma gondii, Cryptosporidium parvum, Babesia spp., Eimeria spp., and Neospora caninum) with substantial global health and economic impact. Resistance to key chemotherapeutics, including the partner and antifolate drugs used against several of these diseases, is narrowing a limited arsenal of target-specific treatments, creating an urgent need for mechanistically distinct drug targets. Proteolytic enzymes are attractive candidates, yet antiprotease drug discovery in the Apicomplexa has concentrated on aspartyl and cysteine proteases, leaving zinc metalloproteases (ZMPs) comparatively neglected despite non-redundant roles in haemoglobin digestion, invasion, egress, organelle biogenesis, and immune evasion. This review synthesises the biology, conservation, and drug-target status of apicomplexan ZMPs (MEROPS families M1, M16C, M17, M18, M24, M41) across the six species above. Catalytic-domain conservation, genetic and pharmacological validation status, and inhibitor pharmacology (hydroxamic acid, phosphinic acid, bestatin, amino-benzosuberone, and peptide-based scaffolds) are compared family-by-family. A multi-criteria druggability framework identifies the M17 leucyl aminopeptidase and apicoplast-resident FtsH1 (M41) as the most compelling pan-apicomplexan targets, reflecting genetic essentiality, chemical tractability, and host selectivity, while the expanded M16C insulinase family of C. parvum illustrates a lineage-specific opportunity. Principal gaps include sparse genetic validation outside P. falciparum and T. gondii, near-total absence of experimental structures beyond P. falciparum, and no ZMP inhibitor yet advanced to in vivo or clinical testing. This synthesis aims to advance apicomplexan zinc metalloproteases from an underexplored genomic feature toward a validated class of antiparasitic drug targets.

papers.title: Tick-borne diseases in French Guiana: A comprehensive review pinpointing differences from mainland France.
papers.abstract: French Guiana (FG), an Amazonian French territory, represents a unique ecological and epidemiological setting for tick-borne diseases (TBDs). In contrast to mainland France, where TBDs are well-documented, data from FG remain scarce. We carried out a systematic review using the PRISMA criteria for our search of the PubMed, ScienceDirect, and SciELO data bases. We identified 68 articles, of which 43 met our inclusion criteria. Data from FG were compared with those originating from mainland France. Albeit highly prevalent in Europe, and notwithstanding detection of a distinct Borrelia species in bird-associated ticks, there have been no confirmed autochthonous cases of Lyme disease in French Guiana. Conversely, Q fever occurs more frequently in this overseas territory than in mainland France, even though its causative agent, Coxiella burnetii, has been detected only one time in a local tick. While Rickettsia spp. are widely present in tick populations, no human rickettsiosis has been reported. As for Anaplasma and Ehrlichia spp., they have been identified in wildlife, domestic animals, and ticks, but with only one documented human case of chronic anaplasmosis, which was caused by a novel species, Candidatus Anaplasma sparouinense. Other pathogens, including Babesia, Bartonella, and filarial nematodes, have been detected in animals or ticks, but without evidence of human infection. Of note, emerging conditions have been described, one example being alpha-gal syndrome, an allergy triggered by tick bites to mammalian meat. To summarize, available data remain limited, and in all likelihood, the burden of TBDs in FG is underestimated. Integrated research combining human, animal and environmental surveillance is needed to more precisely characterize epidemiology, assess risks, and facilitate preventive strategies.

papers.title: Public awareness of alpha-gal syndrome and tick bite prevention practices, United States, Fall 2023.
papers.abstract: Alpha-gal syndrome (AGS) is a unique non-infectious tickborne disease that can develop after a tick bite. AGS can cause severe allergic symptoms (when patients are exposed to alpha-gal) and be challenging for patients to manage because alpha-gal is found in mammalian meat, dairy, and some non-food products. We sought to understand public awareness of AGS, especially relative to other tickborne diseases. We used a 2023 nationally representative survey of adults to investigate public awareness of AGS in the United States and found that knowledge was very low, with 70% of respondents having no prior knowledge of AGS. Respondents with prior AGS knowledge were more concerned about both AGS and infectious tickborne diseases, including Lyme disease, than those without prior AGS knowledge. This study suggests that improving public awareness of AGS could encourage individuals to try to prevent tick bites.

papers.title: Lyme Carditis Beyond Atrioventricular Block: Cardiac Arrest and Transient Atrial Fibrillation With Preserved Atrioventricular Conduction.
papers.abstract: Lyme disease may involve the heart during early dissemination and most commonly produces atrioventricular (AV) conduction abnormalities. PR interval prolongation, therefore, frequently guides clinical suspicion and management. We describe a previously healthy man who presented with seizure-like activity, aborted cardiac arrest, transient atrial fibrillation, and cardiac magnetic resonance findings consistent with acute myocarditis, although AV conduction remained normal. Serologic testing subsequently confirmed Lyme carditis. The patient recovered completely with oral doxycycline. This case illustrates that electrical instability may occur despite preserved PR intervals and reinforces the need for suspicion in patients with compatible systemic features.

papers.title: Untitled
papers.abstract: Post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome (PTLDS) is characterized by persistent symptoms after antibiotic therapy for Borrelia burgdorferi infection. The mechanisms underlying these symptoms remain incompletely understood and have been attributed to ongoing low-level infection, autoimmunity, or immune dysregulation driven by residual bacterial antigens. We investigated whether Borrelia burgdorferi protein antigen persists in long-lived monocyte subsets in PTLDS patients and is associated with broader immune dysregulation. CD14 ⁺ CD16 ⁺ monocytes from 10 patients with PTLDS were analyzed by mass spectrometry; plasma from all 10 was profiled on a 14-plex cytokine panel against 50 healthy donors; PBMCs from 6 patients (3 antigen-positive and 3 antigen-negative) underwent RT-qPCR and bulk RNA-seq with immune-compartment profiling. FlaB and OspC were detected in CD14 ⁺ CD16 ⁺ monocytes months to years after treatment, whereas Borrelia burgdorferi transcript was not detected. Plasma IFN-γ exceeded the healthy donor median in all 10 participants. Antigen-positive samples showed an antigen-associated inflammatory transcriptional profile, including increased TNFSF14/LIGHT, GSDMD, GBP5, and KCNJ2 expression, together with a compartment-level pattern of monocyte-skewed myeloid reconfiguration, higher neutrophil-related features, and selective T-cell-state changes. These findings link residual Borrelia burgdorferi protein in CD14 ⁺ CD16 ⁺ monocytes to monocyte-skewed immune remodeling in PTLDS, paralleling observations in long COVID and supporting a model in which post-infectious syndromes are sustained by antigen-fueled immune remodeling rather than ongoing infection. Many people treated for Lyme disease go on to experience fatigue, pain, and difficulty thinking for months or years, and the reason is unknown. Persistent infection has been a leading explanation, yet longer courses of antibiotics do not help. We found proteins from Borrelia burgdorferi , the bacterium that causes Lyme disease, inside long-lived blood monocytes of patients with lasting symptoms, years after treatment and with no sign that the bacterium was still active. Patients carrying these proteins showed a distinct inflammatory immune profile. These findings point to leftover bacterial material, rather than ongoing infection, as a possible driver of persistent symptoms, echo observations in long COVID, and argue that treatments directed at the immune response deserve study.
papers.journal: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences

papers.title: Mitochondrial proteome of the apicomplexan Babesia divergens.
papers.abstract: Babesia are tick-transmitted apicomplexan parasites of widespread medical and veterinary importance. Although atovaquone, a first-line therapy for human babesiosis, targets one of the three proteins encoded by mitochondrial DNA, a full characterization of the nuclear-encoded mitochondrial proteome is lacking. Here, we combined organelle immunoprecipitation and density gradient separation to enrich mitochondria from Babesia divergens. Using protein mass spectrometry and protein correlation profiling, we generated B. divergens MitoCarta (BdMitoCarta), a high-confidence inventory of 525 mitochondrial proteins. The B. divergens mitoproteome is broadly conserved across Apicomplexa, which, as a clade, have undergone reductive evolution. As seen in other apicomplexans, metabolite transport and the TCA cycle have diverged, with loss of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, presence of malate:quinone oxidoreductase, and a class I fumarate hydratase. Specific to Babesia is the presence of two mitochondrial isocitrate dehydrogenase homologs. Using isolated mitochondria, we performed blue native PAGE complexome analysis and detected previously uncharacterized proteins co-migrating with the ATP synthase and mitochondrial ribosome. Our work has yielded the first mitochondrial proteome and complexome for Babesia, which we expect to be a valuable resource for understanding the evolution of apicomplexan parasites for future therapeutic development.

papers.title: Molecular prevalence and diagnostic gene targets of Anaplasma, Babesia, Theileria, and Trypanosoma in cattle and buffaloes across Southeast Asia (2015-2025): A systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: Hemoparasitic infections caused by Anaplasma, Babesia, Theileria, and Trypanosoma adversely affect cattle and buffalo health, resulting in economic losses and reduced livestock productivity in Southeast Asia. Although numerous molecular epidemiological studies have been conducted in individual countries, a comprehensive regional synthesis of polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-confirmed prevalence and molecular diagnostic targets has been lacking. This study aimed to estimate the pooled molecular prevalence of major hemoparasites in cattle and buffaloes across Southeast Asia, summarize the PCR target genes used for their detection, and investigate the effects of geographical region and host species on prevalence. A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines. PubMed, ScienceDirect, and Scopus were searched for studies published between 2015 and December 31, 2025. Cross-sectional studies conducted in Southeast Asia that used PCR-based methods and reported extractable prevalence data were included. Pooled prevalence estimates were calculated using random-effects meta-analysis. Heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran's Q test and the I² statistic, whereas meta-regression was performed to evaluate the influence of geographical region (mainland versus maritime Southeast Asia) and host species. Publication bias was assessed for Babesia spp. Twenty-two cross-sectional studies involving 5,789 cattle and 901 buffaloes met the inclusion criteria. The pooled prevalence was 12% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 3%-38%) for Anaplasma spp., 18% (95% CI: 11%-28%) for Babesia spp., 11% (95% CI: 3%-35%) for Theileria spp., and 11% (95% CI: 4%-28%) for Trypanosoma evansi. Species-specific pooled prevalences were 5% for Anaplasma marginale, 10% for Babesia bigemina, 9% for Babesia bovis, and 10% for Theileria orientalis. Significant between-study heterogeneity was observed across all analyses. Meta-regression identified a significantly higher prevalence of B. bovis in maritime than mainland Southeast Asia (p = 0.0048), whereas no significant regional or host species effects were detected for the remaining hemoparasites. The review also compiled the principal PCR target genes used for molecular diagnosis, including 16S rRNA, groEL, MSP4, RAP-1a, AMA-1, SBP-2, SBP-4, MSA, MPSP, RoTat 1.2 VSG, ITS1, ITS2, and satellite DNA. Major bovine hemoparasites remain widely distributed across Southeast Asia, highlighting the need for strengthened molecular surveillance and standardized diagnostic approaches. This study provides the first comprehensive regional synthesis of PCR-confirmed prevalence and molecular diagnostic targets for major hemoparasites in cattle and buffaloes, offering valuable evidence to support veterinary diagnostics, surveillance programs, and disease control strategies based on a One Health approach.

papers.title: Genome assembly and gene annotation of Babesia ovis Israeli strain (Piroplasmida: Babesiidae) using PacBio HiFi sequencing.
papers.abstract: Babesia ovis is a unicellular parasite of sheep and goats transmitted by the tick Rhipicephalus bursa. B. ovis infection is widespread and can be lethal, and therefore there is need for a deeper understanding of its biology and pathogenesis. There is currently a single genome available for a clinical isolate of B. ovis, and no laboratory strains have been sequenced so far. In this study we have sequenced and assembled the genome of the Israeli laboratory strain of B. ovis using highly accurate long-read sequencing (PacBio HiFi). The resulting assembly has high contiguity, with the four largest contigs comprising 96% of the assembly and representing putative near-complete chromosomes. Annotation identified 3,549 genes, of which 3,046 (85.6%) could be functionally annotated. BUSCO analysis on the annotated genes revealed 95.5%, 98.8% and 100% completeness of the Aconoidasida, Apicomplexa, and Alveolata lineages, respectively. Comparative analysis with other annotated piroplasmida genomes reveals the vast majority of predicted genes clustered in orthogroups. The availability of a high-quality genome assembly for a tractable laboratory strain could prove impactful in unlocking more basic and applied research avenues to be pursued for this important parasite system.

papers.title: Development of bilateral facial nerve palsies while receiving doxycycline for early disseminated Lyme disease.
papers.abstract: Disease progression is uncommon in patients diagnosed with Lyme disease who receive appropriate therapy. Here we report a case of a patient developing bilateral facial nerve palsies while receiving oral doxycycline therapy for early disseminated Lyme disease and review the literature of similar cases. A 58-year-old previously healthy male from the mid-Atlantic area in the U.S. presented with a multifocal erythematous rash consistent with erythema migrans after international travel. His clinical presentation and two-step Lyme-serology testing confirmed a diagnosis of Lyme disease. Four days into initiation of doxycycline therapy, he developed bilateral facial weakness including difficulty raising the corners of his mouth and lifting his eyebrows bilaterally. He experienced neurologic improvement with ongoing antimicrobial therapy with ceftriaxone and subsequent doxycycline and had complete recovery 7 weeks later. This case describes an uncommon presentation of neuroborreliosis with bilateral facial palsies which developed after initiation of treatment of early disseminated Lyme disease. The manifestations in this case may be due to host immune reaction as seen in other spirochetal diseases. The findings resolved with continued therapy. In our review of the literature, we identified three additional cases of neuroborreliosis which progressed on treatment but also had eventual resolution of signs and symptoms. Clinicians should be aware that facial palsies rarely can occur on therapy for Lyme disease but do not necessarily imply a worse prognosis.

papers.title: Case Report: Atypical cat-scratch disease presenting as referred shoulder pain and deep lymphadenopathy in a pediatric patient.
papers.abstract: Cat-scratch disease (CSD) is a zoonotic infection attributable to Bartonella henselae. Typical clinical manifestations include regional lymphadenopathy accompanied by primary cutaneous lesions that develop following exposure to cats. Although most patients present with typical regional lymphadenopathy, a subset of patients may develop atypical manifestations, which can complicate diagnosis. Owing to the nonspecific clinical features, CSD is prone to misdiagnosis or diagnostic omission. This report describes a pediatric case of atypical cat-scratch disease characterized by initial symptoms of fever and shoulder arthralgia, absence of superficial lymphadenopathy, and involvement of deep lymph nodes. This report aims to broaden clinicians' recognition of the diverse and atypical clinical manifestations of this disease. An 11-year-old female patient presented to the hospital with persistent fever accompanied by left shoulder joint pain and restricted movement of the left upper extremity. Physical examination upon admission revealed no superficial lymphadenopathy or characteristic cutaneous lesions. Following empirical broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy, the patient continued to experience recurrent febrile episodes, with persistently elevated inflammatory markers. Subsequent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the shoulder joint and contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the chest demonstrated multiple enlarged lymph nodes in the left axillary, supraclavicular, and deep cervical regions. Further history-taking disclosed recent exposure to cats. Histopathological examination of an axillary lymph node biopsy (hematoxylin-eosin staining) revealed suppurative granulomatous lymphadenitis. These H&E histopathological findings are merely supportive rather than confirmatory evidence for CSD, as we failed to perform Bartonella henselae-specific serology, PCR, Warthin-Starry silver staining or immunohistochemistry to identify the pathogen directly. The diagnosis was considered highly suggestive of atypical CSD based on integrated clinical, radiological, epidemiological, and histopathological findings. Upon diagnosis, the patient was administered doxycycline in combination with rifampicin for antimicrobial treatment. The patient's body temperature normalized, shoulder pain progressively resolved, and inflammatory markers returned to reference ranges. During a 3-month follow-up period, no disease recurrence was noted. Shoulder joint mobility was restored to normal, and no significant adverse drug reactions were observed. In pediatric patients presenting with fever of unknown origin accompanied by musculoskeletal symptoms, suboptimal response to conventional anti-infective therapy, and absence of superficial lymphadenopathy, the possibility of atypical cat scratch disease should be considered. A detailed assessment of contact history with domestic animals, along with prompt deep lymph node imaging evaluation and histopathological biopsy, facilitates early and appropriate clinical diagnosis. Implementation of targeted antimicrobial therapy may improve clinical outcomes in affected children.

papers.title: Untitled
papers.abstract: Dasatinib is a second-generation tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) used in Philadelphia chromosome-positive (Ph+) acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), and chylothorax is one of its rare but serious lymphatic complications. We encountered a 14-year-old boy with Ph + acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) who developed bilateral chylothorax while on dasatinib, with concurrent B. henselae infection (cat-scratch disease) confirmed in the pleural fluid. Prompted by this index case, we performed a systematic review of the literature to explore the potential association between dasatinib-associated chylothorax and Bartonella henselae infection. We searched multiple databases up to March 2026 and identified 24 cases of TKI-associated chylothorax and 11 cases of leukemia-related cat-scratch disease. In our index case, the pleural fluid triglyceride concentration reached 20.40 mmol/L (≈1806 mg/dL)-the highest value reported to date-and mNGS detected B. henselae together with other organisms. After dasatinib was discontinued and the patient received chest drainage, somatostatin, fasting, and anti-infective therapy with doxycycline plus rifampicin, imaging showed near-complete resolution of the effusion, and repeat mNGS confirmed clearance of B. henselae. A formal causality assessment using the Naranjo scale gave a score of 7, indicating a "probable" adverse drug reaction. This case illustrates that lymphatic and infectious complications can coincide in the same patient. Dasatinib-mediated inhibition of Src family kinases may simultaneously impair lymphatic endothelial integrity and suppress T-cell-mediated immune surveillance, thereby facilitating both chylous leakage and opportunistic infection. Clinicians managing paediatric patients receiving long-term dasatinib therapy should remain vigilant for both lymphatic complications and atypical opportunistic infections.

papers.title: Molecular survey of tick-borne pathogens and other parasites associated with an anemia outbreak in llamas (Lama glama).
papers.abstract: The global expansion of South American camelid farming contrasts with the limited knowledge of the pathogens that can infect them. This study investigated the presence of multiple infectious agents, including Anaplasmataceae, Bartonella sp., hemotropic Mycoplasma, piroplasmids, trypanosomatids, and gastrointestinal parasites, in 10 surviving llamas sampled following an outbreak of clinical anemia. Ehrlichia sp. was molecularly detected in 1/10 animal, hemotropic Mycoplasma sp. in 4/10, and 7/10 were infected with apicomplexans, while parasitological stool analysis showed that 6/9 were infected with Strongyloides sp. Co-infections were detected in 4/10 of the positive animals. All samples tested negative for Anaplasma sp., A. marginale, Bartonella sp., and trypanosomes. Genetic sequencing indicated that the detected Ehrlichia sp. was closely related to 'Candidatus Ehrlichia regneryi', the hemotropic Mycoplasma sp. showed high identity to 'Candidatus Mycoplasma haemolamae', and the apicomplexans were identified as Babesia bovis and Sarcocystis masoni. These findings constitute the first report of B. bovis-like and an Ehrlichia species molecularly detected in llamas, highlighting the diverse range of agents that can circulate in these animals and underscoring the need for a greater understanding of pathogen epidemiology in camelid production.

papers.title: Untitled
papers.abstract: The Fea's muntjac (Muntiacus feae) and the northern red muntjac (Muntiacus vaginalis) are Asian cervids maintained in captive conservation programmes in Thailand, yet information on blood-borne pathogens in these species remains limited. This study aimed to investigate Theileria spp. infection in 34 captive muntjacs from four facilities across Thailand using PCR, Sanger sequencing, phylogenetic analysis, and liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS)-based serum proteomics. All animals appeared clinically healthy, and no hemoparasites were observed on blood smears. Nevertheless, Theileria spp. DNA was detected by PCR in every individual, indicating subclinical infection. Babesia spp. were below the detection limit of the PCR assay, while members of the Anaplasmataceae were not detected. Phylogenetic analysis of 15 sequences positioned most isolates among T. capreoli-associated (9/15) or other cervid-associated Theileria lineages (5/15), while one isolate (1/15) was positioned separately; relationships involving the study isolates were generally weakly supported. Serum proteomics identified 414 Theileria-associated proteins consistently detected in both host species. Functional annotation revealed proteins involved in invasion (rhoptry-associated proteins), proteolysis (aspartyl proteases and calpain-like proteins), ubiquitin-mediated regulation, vesicular trafficking, and RNA processing, providing preliminary functional insight into Theileria-associated biological processes during subclinical infection. These findings suggest a potential role of captive muntjacs in parasite maintenance where competent vectors are present and demonstrate the value of integrating molecular detection with proteomic profiling to investigate host-parasite interactions in wildlife.

papers.title: Untitled
papers.abstract: Borrelia miyamotoi is a relapsing-fever spirochete that conventional tick-borne testing does not detect. We report a case notable for two findings not emphasized in prior series: creatine kinase elevation to 1464 U/L and glucose concentrations above 500 mg/dL without ketoacidosis in a pump-treated patient with type 1 diabetes mellitus. A 36-year-old man with frequent wooded exposure presented with fever, headache, myalgias, and rash, along with leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and mild transaminitis. Lyme serology, Babesia smear, Anaplasma and Ehrlichia PCR, spotted-fever group Rickettsia serology, and blood cultures were negative; blood real-time PCR identified B. miyamotoi after discharge. The hyperglycemia was attributable to infection-related insulin resistance and interruption of pump delivery. Seventeen days of doxycycline produced full clinical and laboratory recovery. Exercise and dehydration may have contributed to the hyperCKemia. This case supports early blood PCR during the febrile illness in culture-negative tick-borne disease and illustrates that insulin requirements may rise sharply when infection coincides with failure of insulin-delivery technology.

papers.title: Masquerade Syndrome Presenting as Optic Neuritis and Retinitis Due to Pituitary Germinoma.
papers.abstract: Masquerade syndrome is a collective term for various ocular diseases presenting with clinical features resembling intraocular inflammation. Delays in definitive diagnosis and treatment can not only lead to irreversible vision loss but also impact the patient's prognosis regarding survival. We report the case of a 26-year-old male patient who presented with impaired vision in the right eye, which had persisted for six months; neuroretinitis was diagnosed. Although infectious neuroretinitis was suspected, tests for pathogens such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Toxoplasma, Toxocara, and Bartonella were all negative. Treatment with betamethasone eye drops alone resulted in a fluctuating course of improvement and worsening of the neuroretinitis. Ten months after the initial visit, the patient's headache-which had begun one month prior-worsened and was accompanied by vomiting and a pulsating sensation, leading to a consultation with our department of neurosurgery. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a lobulated mass extending from the right midbrain to the right thalamus, causing narrowing of the cerebral aqueduct and hydrocephalus. Four days after the neurosurgical consultation, the patient underwent endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV) and a brain biopsy, leading to a definitive diagnosis of germinoma. The headache improved the day after surgery, and by one month after the operation, the hydrocephalus had resolved, while neuroretinitis also showed improvement. The patient received carboplatin and etoposide (CARE) treatment in the second, third, and fourth months post-surgery, whole-ventricle radiotherapy (24 Gy/15 fractions) in the fifth and sixth months, and ifosfamide (IFO), cisplatin (CDDP), and etoposide (VP-16) (ICE) treatment in the seventh, ninth, and 11th months. No recurrence of the brain tumor has been observed since then. At the final follow-up visit five years post-surgery, the neuroretinitis had resolved. When neuroretinitis is observed in a young patient and infectious causes have been ruled out, intracranial germinoma should be considered in the differential diagnosis.

papers.title: Atypical Lyme Neuroborreliosis Presenting With Ventriculitis and Cerebritis: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Lyme neuroborreliosis is a neurological manifestation of infection by Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato and most commonly presents with lymphocytic meningitis, cranial neuropathy, or painful radiculitis. Central nervous system parenchymal involvement is uncommon, and ventriculitis is rarely reported. We describe a man in his late 70s who presented with acute confusion, dysarthria, and left-sided weakness following several days of severe lower-limb pain and progressive mobility impairment. His neurological status rapidly deteriorated, with secondary seizures requiring invasive mechanical ventilation and intensive care support. Laboratory evaluation demonstrated a marked systemic inflammatory response, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury, and cholestatic liver dysfunction. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed pleocytosis with initial neutrophilic predominance, markedly elevated protein, and preserved glucose. Routine bacterial cultures and molecular testing for common central nervous system pathogens were negative. Anti-Borrelia IgG and IgM antibodies were detected in CSF, although a paired CSF-serum antibody index was unavailable. Brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated inflammatory material within the occipital horns of the lateral ventricles, bilateral leptomeningeal involvement, and focal parenchymal lesions with restricted diffusion suggestive of cerebritis. In the appropriate clinical context, these findings supported a diagnosis of probable Lyme neuroborreliosis with an unusual ventriculitis-like presentation. Despite prolonged antimicrobial therapy and partial improvement in CSF and radiological inflammatory findings, neurological recovery remained limited, and the patient subsequently died following ventilator-associated pneumonia complicated by septic shock. This case illustrates an uncommon and severe central nervous system presentation potentially associated with Lyme neuroborreliosis and highlights both the diagnostic value and limitations of CSF serology when demonstration of intrathecal antibody synthesis is unavailable.

papers.title: Cat scratch disease with fever and lymphadenopathy without definite cat exposure diagnosed via tissue metagenomic next-generation sequencing technology: a case report.
papers.abstract: Cat scratch disease (CSD), a disease caused by Bartonella henselae (B. henselae), is often associated with exposure to cats. However, in rare cases, a history of cat exposure is absent, and thus achieving a definitive diagnosis may be challenging. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) is a relatively new technology that can analyze pathogens without introducing inherent biases. In this report, we describe a case of CSD diagnosed via mNGS, which supports the use of mNGS in identifying rare types of pathogenic infection. A 54-year-old male exhibited fever and headache of unknown cause, with a history of working at a chicken farm and no clear cat exposure. Routine antibiotic treatment for infection was ineffective. Lymph node biopsy demonstrated granulomas accompanied by chronic suppurative inflammation and abscess formation. A biopsy sample from the parotid lymph node was subjected to mNGS, which revealed the presence of B. henselae and led to a subsequent diagnosis of CSD. After treatment with azithromycin, the patient recovered and was discharged. At the 3-month telephone follow-up, the patient was asymptomatic. CSD in patients with prolonged fever plus culture-negative granulomatous lymphadenopathy or similar compatible findings, even when the exposure history is atypical，and mNGS, as an effective examination method, can aid in arriving at a definitive diagnosis.

papers.title: Broad-spectrum molecular detection of zoonotic agents in wild micromammals: a nationwide surveillance study in the Republic of Korea.
papers.abstract: Wild micromammals serve as key hosts for diverse zoonotic pathogens, maintaining these agents in natural ecosystems and facilitating potential spillover to humans. Assessing pathogen prevalence in micromammals is essential for evaluating zoonotic risk and informing public health interventions. In this study, we applied the TaqMan Array Card (TAC) platform, a high-throughput molecular diagnostic tool, to micromammal-borne zoonotic pathogen surveillance. From October to November 2022, a total of 160 wild micromammals, including Apodemus agrarius (Striped field mouse) (90.6, n = 145) and Crocidura lasiura (Ussuri white-toothed shrew) (9.4%, n = 15), were collected from 12 regions. Spleen tissues were screened for 45 viral, bacterial, and protozoan pathogens using the TAC platform. Viral pathogens were detected at lower frequencies, including Junin virus (2.5%, n = 4) and lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (0.6%, n = 1). In contrast, bacterial pathogens showed high prevalence, including Bartonella spp. (78.8%, n = 126), Ehrlichia spp. (47.5%, n = 76), Anaplasma spp. (46.9%, n = 75), Borrelia spp. (36.3%, n = 58), Orientia tsutsugamushi (25.6%, n = 41), Rickettsia spp. (4.4%, n = 7), and Leptospira spp. (2.5%, n = 4) as well as protozoan pathogens such as Trypanosoma spp. (87.5%, n = 140), Cryptosporidium (20.0%, n = 32), and Toxoplasma gondii (1.3%, n = 2). However, some detections particularly viral pathogens were based solely on the TAC platform and were not confirmed by conventional PCR and sequencing. Phylogenetic analyses of TAC-positive samples revealed the presence of diverse zoonotic agents, including Anaplasma phagocytophilum, Ehrlichia muris, Candidatus Ehrlichia khabarensis, Candidatus Neoehrlichia mikurensis, Borreliella afzelii, Borrelia miyamotoi, O. tsutsugamushi Saitama and Young-worl strains, Bartonella quintana, B. fuyuanensis, and B. japonica. These findings demonstrate the widespread regional distribution of micromammal-borne zoonotic pathogens across the ROK and provide essential baseline data to support integrated One Health surveillance frameworks for emerging and re-emerging micromammal-borne zoonoses.
